strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in active view selection: repeatedly fitting a neural rendering model. Predicting per-view error maps with a feedforward network provides a plausible way to reduce online computation.
The reported selection-time reduction is substantial: approximately 0.5 minutes versus 175–198 minutes for selecting 20 views, with lower memory requirements on the same hardware.

Evaluation includes NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, image-quality and geometry-related metrics, three runs, and held-out categories. The reported 3DGS improvement over NVF is particularly promising: 36.71 versus 30.67 PSNR.
The proposed dataset contains 62,400 image–uncertainty-map pairs, and ablations investigate supervision metrics, selection policies, and training-data diversity.
weaknesses: The central selection rule is underspecified and appears inconsistent with its supervision. UPNet predicts PSNR, but Equation 2 maximizes the product of predicted values, whereas higher PSNR indicates lower reconstruction error. Removing values below 0.1 also lacks an explanation on the PSNR scale. Figure 3 explicitly states that normalization is not used during training or inference. A precise transformation from PSNR/SSIM to nonnegative uncertainty is essential to reproduce and assess the method.

Essential baselines are missing: random selection, uniform spherical sampling, farthest-point coverage, and a fixed or average uncertainty map. Without these, the experiments do not establish that image-conditioned uncertainty prediction improves over inexpensive coverage strategies. Comparisons also omit the learned next-best-view approaches discussed in related work and recent Gaussian-based selectors, weakening both novelty and efficiency positioning.

The claim of matching an all-views upper bound with half the views is not supported. Table 1 shows PSNR gaps of 3.28 dB in-domain and 2.17 dB out-of-domain, alongside perceptual-quality gaps. Moreover, the reference trains directly on the evaluation images; it measures training-view fitting rather than held-out novel-view synthesis. A separate 40-view training baseline evaluated on disjoint views is needed.

The main NeRF improvements are modest and uncertain. In-domain PSNR is 33.19 ± 1.74 versus NVF's 33.08 ± 0.44, and MSE is essentially unchanged. No paired statistical analysis establishes a reliable improvement. The assertion of outperforming every baseline across all metrics is also inaccurate: out-of-domain completion ratio is lower than NVF's. Results only at a 20-view budget do not establish improved sample efficiency or minimal-view reconstruction.

The ablation protocol is unclear: the default method achieves 37.41 PSNR in Tables 4/S2, compared with 33.19 in the main in-domain NeRF experiment, without explaining the changed evaluation setting. Ablations lack uncertainty estimates and do not compare multiplication against alternative history-aware aggregators. Independent single-view reconstruction errors are not demonstrated to represent information gain after multiple observations.

Generalization evidence is limited to synthetic, centered ShapeNet objects at a fixed camera radius, with only 10 objects in each of two unseen categories. Interpolation from 48 fixed anchors supports flexible sampling on this sphere, but broader arbitrary-viewpoint claims are not validated. The Splatter-Image pretraining split and its overlap with evaluation objects/categories are unspecified.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the promised release. The main text specifies 80 training instances per category, while Figure S1 describes 90. The ViT variant, initial-view protocol, mesh evaluation thresholds, and important baseline optimization details are missing. Offline dataset-generation and training costs are unreported, so the substantial timing advantage should be interpreted specifically as online selection savings.

strengths: The method addresses a practical bottleneck: repeated reconstruction during active view selection. Predicting view-dependent error maps with a feedforward network is a useful approach to reducing online computation.
The reported results are promising, particularly the 3DGS improvement over NVF (36.71 versus 30.67 PSNR) and selection-time reduction from 175–198 minutes to approximately 0.5 minutes.

The paper contributes a substantial synthetic supervision dataset and evaluates selected views with two reconstruction backbones, image and geometry metrics, held-out categories, and several component ablations. Supplementary results include variability over three runs.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty definition is incomplete and potentially inconsistent with the selection algorithm. UPNet predicts PSNR-based targets, but the policy maximizes their product and removes values below 0.1. Raw PSNR increases with reconstruction quality, whereas the policy requires larger values to indicate greater uncertainty. No conversion is specified, and Figure 3 explicitly states that normalization is not used during training or inference. The direction and scale of this transformation are essential to understanding and reproducing the method.

The comparisons do not establish the value of learned, object-dependent selection. Random, uniform spherical, farthest-point, and average-map baselines are missing, as are comparisons with the supervised or reinforcement-learning selectors discussed in related work. These inexpensive alternatives are particularly important when the principal advantage is speed. PUN also resamples its candidate set at each step while competing methods use fixed candidates, introducing an additional experimental difference.

The repeated claim of matching the upper bound is not supported by Table 1: PUN trails it by 3.28 dB in-domain and 2.17 dB out-of-domain. Moreover, the designated upper bound trains on the evaluation images themselves; although disclosed, this measures training-view reconstruction rather than held-out synthesis and does not establish that half as many acquisition views suffice. Performance-versus-view-count curves and a larger-view baseline evaluated on disjoint test views are needed.

The NeRF evidence is weaker than the narrative suggests. In-domain PSNR improves over NVF by only 0.11 dB, compared with PUN's reported standard deviation of 1.74 dB; SSIM and completion ratio tie at the reported precision. Out-of-domain completion ratio is lower than NVF's. Thus, the claim of consistent superiority across all metrics is inaccurate. The ablation default also reports 37.41 PSNR rather than the main experiment's 33.19, without explaining the evaluation-setting difference.

The justification for treating predicted single-view reconstruction errors as multi-view information gain is limited. Multiplying independently predicted maps does not explicitly model how observations jointly resolve uncertainty. There is no quantitative validation of candidate ranking or correlation with actual reconstruction improvement, and no comparison against straightforward alternative aggregation rules such as minimum or mean. Consequently, the contribution beyond error regression, spherical interpolation, and heuristic aggregation remains insufficiently established.

Generalization and reproducibility remain limited. Experiments cover only synthetic, centered ShapeNet objects at a fixed camera radius, with just 20 objects across two held-out categories. The relationship between Splatter-Image's pretraining data and the evaluation objects/categories is unspecified. The exact ViT configuration, uncertainty transformation, baseline initialization, and ablation protocol need clarification; Figure S1 also describes 90 training instances per category whereas the main text specifies 80 plus 10 validation instances. Offline dataset-generation and training costs are not quantified, so the substantial reported speedup should be interpreted specifically as online selection speed.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: selecting 20 views takes approximately 0.5 minutes versus 175–198 minutes for the evaluated baselines, with considerably lower memory consumption.

Transfer across reconstruction models is promising. In Table 3, PUN improves 3DGS reconstruction PSNR from NVF’s 30.67 to 36.71 dB. Evaluation includes image quality, geometry, and visibility metrics, with three-run variability reported for the principal comparisons.
The 62,400 image–uncertainty-map pairs could provide a useful resource. Ablations examine uncertainty targets, aggregation policies, and training-data composition.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty definition is internally inconsistent. UPNet is trained to predict PSNR, but Equation 2 maximizes the product of predicted values, although higher PSNR indicates lower reconstruction error. The method also removes values below 0.1, while Figure 3 explicitly states that no normalization is used during training or inference. An explicit transformation from PSNR to uncertainty is essential; as written, the selection rule appears to favor well-reconstructed views and the threshold lacks a meaningful scale.

The comparisons do not establish the benefit of learned uncertainty over inexpensive alternatives. Random sampling, uniform spherical coverage, farthest-point selection, and an image-independent average uncertainty map are missing, as are comparisons with supervised next-best-view predictors and recent Gaussian-based methods discussed in the introduction. Comparing efficiency only against methods that repeatedly fit NeRF leaves the main quality–efficiency advantage insufficiently established.

The repeated claim of matching the all-views upper bound is unsupported by Table 1. PUN trails it by 3.28 dB in-domain and 2.17 dB out-of-domain, with materially worse MSE and LPIPS. Moreover, this reference trains directly on the evaluation images; it is an explicitly disclosed in-sample reference, not a standard 40-view generalization baseline. A disjoint 40-view training baseline and quality-versus-view-budget curves are needed to support the claimed view efficiency.

Evidence for consistent superiority is weaker than the narrative suggests. In-domain NeRF PSNR improves over NVF by only 0.11 dB, compared with reported standard deviations of 1.74 and 0.44 dB; SSIM and completion ratio tie at the reported precision. Out-of-domain completion ratio is lower than NVF’s. Paired per-object results would help determine whether the smaller improvements are reliable.

The connection between single-image reconstruction error and the marginal benefit of an additional view is not validated. Multiplying independently predicted single-view maps is a heuristic, without evidence that it estimates residual uncertainty after multiview reconstruction. Quantitative ranking accuracy, correlation with actual reconstruction gains, and an oracle-map comparison would strengthen this central premise.

Generalization is evaluated only on synthetic, centered ShapeNet objects at a fixed camera radius, with just two held-out categories and 20 out-of-domain instances. Arbitrary-viewpoint support is interpolation between 48 anchors on this constrained sphere. These experiments do not establish robustness to real images, pose errors, or broader camera distributions.

Important reproducibility details remain unresolved: the PSNR transformation, precise ViT variant and Splatter-Image checkpoint/training overlap, and baseline fitting schedules. The default ablation result of 37.41 dB also differs substantially from the main in-domain result of 33.19 dB without a clear explanation of the evaluation subset or configuration. These gaps prevent a confident assessment despite the promising reported results.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in active reconstruction: repeatedly fitting a radiance field to select the next view. Predicting view scores directly from images provides a useful approach to amortizing this cost.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: selecting 20 views takes approximately 0.5 minutes versus 175–198 minutes for the iterative baselines. The paper also distinguishes selection time from subsequent reconstruction time.

Experiments cover held-out instances and categories, lighting and distance changes, multiple reconstruction backbones, and selected real-world scenes. Particularly encouraging results include 34.74 versus 33.15 dB on NUM-cat and 36.71 versus 30.67 dB with 3DGS, compared with NVF.

The proposed dataset contains 62,400 image–map pairs, and the paper includes useful ablations of supervision metrics, aggregation policies, training-data composition, anchor density, and redundancy thresholds.
weaknesses: The core selection rule is insufficiently specified and appears inconsistent with its supervision. UPNet predicts PSNR, but the algorithm maximizes the product of predicted values and removes values below 0.1. Higher PSNR indicates lower reconstruction error, so an explicit inversion and normalization are necessary. Neither is described; Figure S4 shows scores roughly in the 10–30 range, while Figure 3 specifies normalization for visualization only. This omission prevents reproducing and assessing the central algorithm.

The repeated claim of matching the upper bound with half the views is not supported by Table 1: PUN trails it by 3.28 dB on NUM-inst and 2.17 dB on NUM-cat, with appreciable MSE and LPIPS gaps. Moreover, the upper-bound model trains on the same 40 images used for evaluation. This is an explicitly acknowledged training-view reference, not a controlled comparison of novel-view generalization or evidence that half as many acquisition views suffice.

Comparisons do not adequately establish novelty or competitiveness against efficient alternatives. The learned and pretrained reconstruction-based selectors discussed in the introduction are absent from experiments, and runtime comparisons only use expensive iterative methods. Uniform sampling is included in supplementary results but omitted from important backbone-transfer and real-scene comparisons. An image-independent average uncertainty map and a simple angular-diversity selector would help establish whether the learned image-conditioned maps provide value beyond a coverage prior.

Single-view reconstruction error is not necessarily the marginal benefit of acquiring a view given multiple observations. Multiplying independent single-image predictions does not model complementary evidence or reconstruction progress. The reported correlation with teacher errors and image complexity supports error prediction, but does not validate conditional information gain or the claimed backbone-independent notion of uncertainty.

The geometry evaluation contains a substantive inconsistency. Completion ratio is defined using reconstructed-to-ground-truth distances, which measures precision rather than completeness. Furthermore, an average distance of 0.35 cm and only 18% of those distances below 5 cm cannot both hold under the stated definitions. The units, distance direction, and implementation need correction before geometry-related claims can be trusted.

Evidence for broad superiority is uneven. On NUM-inst, the PSNR improvement over NVF is only 0.11 dB, while PUN's reported standard deviation is 1.74 dB. PUN does not outperform every baseline across all eight metrics, contrary to the text; for example, NVF has better completion ratio on NUM-cat. Real-world evaluation covers only four selected MIP360 scenes, and the mapping from the spherical candidate-selection procedure to available captured cameras, including exclusion of test images, is not explained.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the exact ViT variant, initial-view policy, and several reconstruction and selection settings. The ablation tables report materially different default results without clearly identifying their evaluation subsets. These gaps, together with the uncertainty-score ambiguity, make the reported gains difficult to independently verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in active view selection: repeatedly fitting a reconstruction model. Predicting viewpoint scores directly from images is a useful approach to reducing online computation.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: selecting 20 views takes approximately 0.5 minutes versus 175–198 minutes for the iterative baselines. The paper also reports the additional reconstruction time.

The evaluation includes held-out instances and categories, multiple reconstruction backbones, lighting and distance changes, and real scenes. Particularly promising results include 36.71 versus 30.67 PSNR for NVF with the 3DGS reconstruction backbone.

The NUM dataset and ablations on aggregation, supervision metrics, training diversity, and anchor density provide useful contributions. The reported prediction–target correlation of 0.82 supports the feasibility of learning reconstruction-error maps.
weaknesses: The central selection rule is underspecified and appears inconsistent with its supervision. Section 3.1 trains UPNet on PSNR, where larger values indicate better reconstruction, while Section 3.3 maximizes the product of predicted uncertainties and removes values below 0.1. The necessary inversion, normalization, and output constraints are not explained; Figure 3 explicitly describes normalization as visualization-only. These details determine whether the algorithm selects informative views and are essential for reproduction.

The repeated claim of matching the upper bound is unsupported by the reported image-quality results. On NUM-inst, PUN achieves 33.19 versus 36.47 PSNR, with MSE 6.96 versus 4.11; on NUM-cat, PSNR is 34.74 versus 36.91. Furthermore, the upper-bound model trains on the same 40 images used for evaluation. This is a disclosed training-view reference, but it does not establish equivalent novel-view performance using half the acquisition budget.

The geometry evaluation contains a serious definition/reporting inconsistency. CR is defined using reconstructed-to-ground-truth distances, which measures proximity of reconstructed points rather than completeness of the ground-truth surface. Moreover, an average distance of approximately 0.35 cm is incompatible with only approximately 18% of those same points lying within 5 cm. The metric direction, units, or implementation must be corrected before the geometric conclusions can be trusted.

Comparisons do not adequately establish the contribution relative to efficient alternatives. The evaluated learned baselines require iterative NeRF fitting, while the cited pretrained reconstruction and direct next-view prediction approaches are not evaluated. Recent Gaussian-based selection methods are also absent. Uniform sampling is included, but stronger inexpensive controls such as farthest-point sampling and an object-independent average uncertainty map would help isolate the value of image-conditioned prediction.

Claims of consistently outperforming every baseline across all eight metrics overstate the evidence. On NUM-inst, the PSNR improvement over NVF is only 0.11 dB, against a reported PUN standard deviation of 1.74 dB. On NUM-cat, NVF has better CR, while uniform sampling ties PUN on several geometry and coverage metrics. Paired uncertainty estimates would help distinguish reliable improvements from small numerical differences.

The interpretation of predicted reconstruction error as multi-view information gain is insufficiently validated. Multiplying single-image error predictions does not explicitly model the joint information provided by acquired views. Correlations between teacher reconstruction errors and visual complexity do not demonstrate calibrated uncertainty or marginal reconstruction improvement. Direct validation against actual gains from candidate views, together with an oracle-map comparison, would strengthen this central premise.

Generalization and reproducibility remain limited. Real-scene evidence uses four selected MIP360 scenes, with low absolute reconstruction quality, and the mapping from the spherical candidate policy to available recorded camera poses is unclear. The precise ViT configuration and initial-view protocol are also unspecified. These limitations, together with the unresolved scoring and metric definitions, prevent the promising efficiency results from establishing a sufficiently convincing top-tier contribution.

strengths: The problem is practically important, and predicting viewpoint scores directly from images offers a clear way to avoid expensive reconstruction updates during acquisition.
Reported efficiency gains are substantial: selecting 20 views takes 0.5 minutes versus 175–198 minutes for the evaluated neural-rendering baselines, with considerably lower memory consumption.
The results provide promising evidence of transfer across reconstruction backbones. On NUM-3DGS-recon, PUN achieves 36.71 dB versus NVF’s 30.67 dB; improvements also appear with Binocular3DGS.
The study includes a sizable supervision dataset, held-out categories, lighting and camera-distance variations, real-scene experiments, and multiple component ablations.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty computation is underspecified. PSNR increases with reconstruction quality, whereas the algorithm maximizes uncertainty and removes values below 0.1. The manuscript does not specify the transformation from PSNR to the uncertainty values used for training, filtering, and multiplication; Figure 3 describes normalization for visualization only. This omission prevents faithful reproduction of the core algorithm.

The repeated claim of matching the upper bound with half the views is unsupported. Table 1 shows PSNR gaps of 3.28 dB on NUM-inst and 2.17 dB on NUM-cat, with substantially worse MSE. Moreover, the upper-bound model trains on the evaluation images themselves, so this is an explicitly in-sample reference rather than a conventional held-out all-view reconstruction comparison.

Comparisons do not establish competitiveness against the most relevant efficient alternatives. The paper discusses learned next-best-view predictors, pretrained reconstruction approaches, and recent active Gaussian methods but does not evaluate them. Timing comparisons against expensive iterative NeRF methods demonstrate amortization benefits without isolating the contribution of the proposed uncertainty maps. Random, farthest-point, and image-independent average-map controls would also help.

The geometric evaluation has a serious definition or reporting inconsistency. Accuracy is defined as mean reconstructed-to-ground-truth distance in centimeters, and completion ratio uses the same distances with a 5 cm threshold. A mean distance of 0.35 cm implies at least approximately 93% within that threshold, incompatible with the reported ratios around 0.18. Additionally, this direction measures precision rather than ground-truth completeness.

Several superiority claims exceed the evidence. On NUM-inst, the PSNR improvement over NVF is only 0.11 dB against reported standard deviations of 1.74 and 0.44 dB. Table S1 shows no uniform advantage across geometric and coverage metrics, and Table S5 shows worse completion and coverage on NeRFAssets.

The real-scene protocol is insufficiently explained: the general procedure samples arbitrary spherical viewpoints, but MIP360 supplies only captured images. Candidate-to-image mapping and explicit exclusion of held-out images from acquisition need clarification. Evaluation covers only four selected scenes, with low absolute reconstruction quality, limiting broad real-world generalization claims.

Multiplying single-image reconstruction-error predictions is a plausible heuristic, but its relationship to conditional multi-view information gain is not established. Correlations with image complexity do not demonstrate that it captures the benefit of acquiring a view after multiple observations. Together with the missing efficient baselines and protocol ambiguities, this leaves insufficient evidence for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
